question: Find a PubMed paper about levetiracetam while breastfeeding, retrieve its abstract, and summarize only the study design, population and findings actually available. Distinguish drug exposure from infant outcomes.
criteria: Fetch abstract before summarizing findings. Direct article link; supported population/design/findings only. Missing abstract or fields disclosed, not filled from memory. Exposure not equivalent to infant outcome or universal safety.
answer:
**Paper:** *Levetiracetam in lactation: How much is excreted into human breast milk?* (2022), PMID 34131926. [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34131926/)

- **Study design:** A study of breast-milk excretion and its relationship to maternal oral dose and serum concentrations. Participants completed a questionnaire; researchers measured levetiracetam in serial breast-milk samples from before dosing through 12 hours afterward and in one pre-dose maternal serum sample. [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34131926/)
- **Population:** The returned metadata lists the source population as **lactation and infant**. The study included 20 breastfeeding women with epilepsy and 21 infants; one woman had twins, 16 infants were fully breastfed, and five were partially breastfed. Infant ages, gestational ages, and prematurity status were not provided in the abstract. [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34131926/)
- **Measured drug exposure:** The mean trough breast-milk/serum ratio was 0.98 ± 0.20. The abstract reported higher estimated infant exposure and relative infant exposure among fully breastfed infants than partially breastfed infants. Maternal dose, maternal serum and breast-milk trough concentrations, and breast-milk AUC values were substantially correlated. [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34131926/)
- **Observed infant outcomes:** Three women reported somnolence in their fully breastfed infants; the abstract states that this resolved shortly after switching to partial breastfeeding. All infants gained weight according to age. The authors described the somnolence as potentially related to breast-milk levetiracetam exposure, but this was an interpretation of an observed association, not proof of causation. [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34131926/)
- **Evidence limitation:** Only the abstract was retrieved. It does not provide the study’s full methods, statistical details, or long-term infant outcomes. The PubMed record lists free full text, but the full text was not retrieved. [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34131926/)

results.title: Levetiracetam in lactation: How much is excreted into human breast milk?
results.abstract: In breastfeeding women, anti-epileptic therapy can lead to infant toxicities, even with newer anti-epileptic drugs such as levetiracetam. This study assessed levetiracetam breastmilk excretion and its correlation with the maternal oral dose and serum concentrations. Women with epilepsy treated with levetiracetam were recruited to this study and completed a questionnaire. Levetiracetam concentrations were determined in serial breastmilk samples (pre-dose to 12 h post-dose period) and in a single pre-dose maternal serum sample. Twenty breastfeeding women and 21 infants (one woman with twins; 16 fully and five partially breastfed infants) participated in this study. The trough breastmilk/serum ratio of levetiracetam was 0.98 ± 0.20. The infant levetiracetam daily dose was 5.39 ± 1.96 and 2.70 ± 0.98 mg. kg-1. d-1 , and the relative infant dose (RID) was 13.8 ± 3.1% and 6.9 ± 1.6% in the fully and partially breastfed infants, respectively. Substantial correlations between the levetiracetam dose, maternal serum and breastmilk trough concentrations, and breastmilk AUC values were found. Three women reported somnolence in their fully breastfed infants, which resolved shortly after switching to partial breastfeeding. All the infants gained weight according to their age. Infant levetiracetam exposure via the breastmilk was close to the safety thresholds (trough breastmilk/serum ratio slightly below 1, RID > 10% in fully breastfed infants), and infant somnolescence reports could be related to exposure of the infants to levetiracetam via breastmilk. Further studies are warranted to reveal the short- and long-term safety of levetiracetam in breastfeeding.
